summary:
Morelos is a state of Mexico, and the sources vetted for this record carry no Morelos-specific statute, enforcement incident or lethality figure. The operative framework is national. Mexico legislates legal gender recognition state by state, and the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation has set binding guidelines for the states, extending the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. Human Rights Watch warned on 31 March 2025 that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

As of March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states with a legislated administrative recognition procedure, two more states operating one in practice without enactment, and six state legislatures that had enacted nothing. Only seven states extend recognition to children. Where no procedure exists, mismatched identity documents drive discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents documented in Guanajuato and Tabasco. A visitor to Morelos is therefore measured against this national position rather than against any locally enacted guarantee.

What legal silence costs on the ground is set out in the Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, which examined a Mexican state without a recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance that draws scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The reporting period covers the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, in a country where more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. Set against that, transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some state statutes: Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months, and a trans woman was found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 for that year.

The comparison across states is the central turbulence: 22 states with legislated procedures against six with none, two running procedures without legislation, and only seven extending recognition to minors. Human Rights Watch has called on the states lacking procedures to adopt them.
localsOnly:
A trans resident of Morelos stands under the national framework, including the binding guidelines issued by the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation in 2022, which apply to all 32 states and extend recognition to minors; the Inter-American Court's requirement of a simple, accessible procedure binds Mexico as a party.

Residents of states with no recognition procedure report that mismatched documents exclude them from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and that each document request carries risk of harassment, and the same barriers surface in banking, health care and police contacts where recognition is delayed or refused.

Homicide impunity exceeded 95% nationally in 2022, and state-level transfemicide statutes remain uneven, with the capital's July 2024 statute the named example. Same-sex marriage has been available to residents nationwide since 2009.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Morelos has enacted an administrative legal gender-recognition procedure, or operates one in practice without legislation, is not stated in the vetted sources. The six states that have enacted nothing and the two running procedures without enactment are not named, so Morelos cannot be placed in any of those groups on this evidence.

Whether Morelos is among the seven states extending recognition to children is not sourced here. No Morelos-specific transfeminicide count, police-conduct incident, document-refusal case, facilities or bathroom rule, or hate-crime protection appears in the inventory; those questions remain open rather than answered in the negative.

The national homicide and transfeminicide figures are country-wide counts and are not broken down for Morelos, and the named cases cited here occurred in other states.
